what: BILL Holdings automates how small businesses pay bills and get paid. Its software receives invoices, routes them for approval, makes the payment, and handles the accounting entry — replacing a process most small firms still do with paper cheques, spreadsheets and email.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, reached directly and through accounting firms and financial institutions that offer the product to their own clients. It also provides corporate cards and expense management.
money: Monthly software fees for accounts payable and receivable automation.
Fees on payments processed, including card and cross-border payments.
Interest earned on customer money held briefly between payment and settlement.
moat: Once a business routes its payments and approvals through BILL, the vendor list, approval rules, payment history and accounting integration all live there, and moving means rebuilding the whole process. Distribution through accounting firms is a genuine advantage: accountants recommend the software to many clients at once, which is far cheaper than acquiring small businesses individually.
risks: Twenty analysts average a $63.30 target against a $63.98 price — effectively no upside, which is an unusual signal of caution from the sell side.
Reported net income of $52.0M against a negative net margin and 181.9 times EV/EBITDA means the earnings figures are not usable for valuation.
Payment volume growth has slowed, and the small business customers it serves are sensitive to economic conditions.
Well-funded private competitors including Ramp and Brex are attacking the same customers aggressively with corporate cards as the entry point.
Interest on held funds is a meaningful part of profit and falls when interest rates fall, which is outside management’s control.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $413.7M against a $5.5B market value is a 7.5% yield, and the shares trade at about 13.3 times free cash flow.
Cash of $1.9B against $1.9B of debt is a balanced position with substantial liquidity.
Revenue has grown strongly, from $642.0M in 2022 to $1.7B in 2026.
Payment automation is deeply embedded once adopted, because the vendor list, approval rules and accounting integration all live in the software.
Most small businesses still pay bills manually, so the market being addressed remains largely unconverted.
watch: Payment volume and take rate, plus net revenue retention. The subscription fee is small; the money is made on payments, so volume and the fee kept on each one are the business.
view: The problem BILL solves is unglamorous and enormous. Most small businesses in America still pay their suppliers with cheques, track approvals by email, and enter everything into their accounting system by hand. BILL replaces that with software that receives the invoice, routes the approval, makes the payment and books the entry. The market is almost entirely unconverted, which is why revenue went from $642 million to $1.7 billion in four years.

The economics are better than the subscription model suggests, and this is worth understanding properly. Subscription fees are a modest quarter of revenue; most of the money comes from fees on the payments processed, which means revenue scales with the dollars flowing through rather than with the number of customers. A further slice comes from interest earned on customer funds held briefly in transit — free income, but income that falls with interest rates and that nobody should capitalise as though it were permanent.

Distribution through accounting firms is the quiet competitive advantage. An accountant who adopts BILL recommends it to dozens of clients, which acquires small businesses at a fraction of what direct selling costs. Acquiring small business customers individually is notoriously expensive, and that channel is why BILL’s unit economics work where many competitors’ do not.

Two things concern me. The first is the competition: Ramp and Brex are extremely well funded, attacking the same customers with corporate cards as the entry point, and intending to work backwards into the payables workflow. The second is the analyst picture — twenty of them averaging a target essentially identical to the share price, which from a group that reliably forecasts upside is as close to a collective shrug as the sell side produces. At 13.3 times free cash flow the price is not demanding, and that is the reason to look. Payment volume, take rate and net retention are where the answer is, and the earnings line should be ignored entirely.
bull: A largely unconverted market keeps adopting payment automation through the accounting-firm channel, payment volume compounds, and 13 times free cash flow is too cheap.
bear: Ramp and Brex take the small business workflow, volume growth slows with a weak small business economy, and falling rates remove the interest income propping up profit.
